title: Wells, Wires and Dots, and What They Do

questions.q: The picture shows bulk material, a quantum well, a quantum wire and a quantum dot; the arrows show where an electron can still move. Why is a quantum well called two-dimensional (2D)?
questions.alt: Four shapes: a cube labelled bulk with arrows in three directions, a flat slab labelled quantum well with arrows in a plane, a thin rod labelled quantum wire with an arrow along it, and a tiny cube labelled quantum dot with no arrows
options: The electron is still free to move in two directions, within the plane of the layer
The electron is trapped in two directions and free in only one
The layer is exactly two atoms thick
The layer gives out light in two directions only
questions.explain: Structures are named by the directions in which the electron is still free. A well is 2D (free in a plane), a wire 1D (free along a line) and a dot 0D (not free at all). Saying a well is 'trapped in two directions' is the common mix-up.

questions.q: True or false: a quantum dot is called one-dimensional (1D).
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. A dot traps the electron in all three directions, leaving it free in none, so it is zero-dimensional (0D). The label counts the free directions.

questions.q: The graphs show the density of states (the number of 'seats' for electrons at each energy) in bulk, a well, a wire and a dot. Why does a quantum-well laser start at a much lower current than a bulk laser?
questions.alt: Four graphs of states available against energy: bulk, a smooth curve rising from zero; well, a staircase; wire, sharp peaks that fall away; dot, single sharp vertical lines
options: The well has a whole step of states right at the bottom, so the injected electrons are not spread over a wide range of energies
The well has more states than bulk at every energy, so it can hold many more electrons for the laser
The well has no states near the bottom, so all the electrons are forced up to one high energy
The well has a single sharp level like an atom, so every electron sits at exactly the same energy
questions.explain: In bulk, injected electrons spread over a wide range of energies and many are wasted. A well's staircase puts a whole step of seats right at the bottom, so the laser starts at a much lower current.

questions.q: Why does a quantum-dot laser barely change its behaviour as it warms up?
options: Its electrons sit on single sharp levels, so warming cannot spread them over a range of energies
Its dots hold so few electrons that the laser makes almost no heat
Its dots are buried in a crystal that carries all the heat away at once
Its band gap grows as it warms, which exactly cancels the warming
questions.explain: A dot's density of states is a set of single sharp levels, like an atom's. Every electron is at one energy, so heat cannot smear them out the way it does in bulk: the laser barely changes as it warms up.

questions.q: A bulk GaAs laser gives out light at 871 nm. What happens to the wavelength if the light comes from a thin GaAs quantum well instead?
options: It gets shorter: the trapped levels sit a little inside the bands, away from the band edges, so the light carries more energy than the gap
It gets longer: the trapped levels sit a little inside the gap, between the band edges, so the light carries less energy than the gap
It stays at 871 nm, because the wavelength is set only by the material, not by the thickness of the layer
It becomes visible green light, because thin layers always give out visible light whatever the material
questions.explain: Electrons and holes in the well sit on trapped levels a little away from their band edges, so the light carries more energy than the band gap: 848 nm for a 10 nm well and 816 nm for a 5 nm well. Thinner well, shorter wavelength.

questions.q: The picture compares an ordinary laser with a quantum cascade laser. Why does a quantum cascade laser need no holes?
questions.alt: Left: in an ordinary laser an electron drops from the conduction band to meet a hole in the valence band. Right: in a quantum cascade laser an electron steps down a series of levels
options: Its electron gives out light by dropping between levels inside the conduction band, not by meeting a hole
It has holes, but they move too slowly to take part, so only the electrons matter
Each electron turns into a hole after its first step and then carries on down
It borrows holes from the metal contacts, so none are needed inside the layers
questions.explain: The electron drops one step, gives out a photon, tunnels into the next step and drops again, all within the conduction band. No holes are needed: the laser is unipolar, and one electron gives many photons.

questions.q: In a quantum cascade laser, what sets the colour (wavelength) of the light?
options: The thickness of the wells, which sets the size of each step
The band gap of the semiconductor, as in an ordinary laser
The voltage applied, which can be tuned to any colour from blue to red
The temperature of the laser, which sets how fast the electrons fall
questions.explain: The step size is set by the well thickness, not the band gap. This lets cascade lasers reach the infrared, a few to tens of micrometres, for sensing tiny traces of gases.

questions.q: How does a HEMT (high-electron-mobility transistor) let electrons move so fast?
options: The donor atoms sit in the AlGaAs, and the electrons travel in the GaAs in a thin sheet away from them
The electrons travel through a vacuum gap between two layers, with nothing to collide with
The channel is cooled to near absolute zero, so the atoms stop vibrating
The electrons are replaced by holes, which move faster in GaAs
questions.explain: Donor atoms supply electrons but also slow them down. In a HEMT the donors are put in the AlGaAs; the electrons fall into the GaAs and travel in a thin sheet away from them: an express lane.

questions.q: The graph shows the conductance of a very short, narrow wire as it is opened up. Why does the conductance rise in equal steps?
questions.alt: A narrow constriction between two wide contacts, and a graph of conductance rising in equal steps (1, 2, 3, 4) as the wire is opened wider
options: Each new 'lane' that opens for the electrons adds the same fixed conductance
Each step is caused by one more impurity being removed from the wire
The wire heats up in steps, and each step lowers its resistance
Each step is one more atom added to the length of the wire
questions.explain: Even a wire too short for electrons to bump into anything has resistance. Like a motorway narrowing to a few lanes, each lane adds a fixed conductance (about 12.9 kΩ of resistance per lane, set at the contacts).

questions.q: What decides whether a carbon nanotube is a metal or a semiconductor?
options: How the graphene sheet is rolled up; about one tube in three is metallic
The length of the tube; long tubes are metals, short tubes semiconductors
The temperature at which the tube is used
The metal catalyst it was grown on, which stays inside the tube
questions.explain: A nanotube is a sheet of graphene rolled into a tube about 1 nm across. The way it is rolled decides metal or semiconductor, and about one tube in three is metallic. Thinner tubes have bigger band gaps.

questions.q: True or false: because electrons cross a short nanotube without bumping into anything, the tube has no resistance and makes no heat.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. A ballistic metallic tube still has about 6.5 kΩ from its two lanes, and heat is made at the contacts.

questions.q: The chart shows the range of colours that colloidal quantum dots of different materials can give out. Why can 3 nm CdSe dots glow green while 3 nm PbS dots glow in the infrared?
questions.alt: Bars of emission wavelength range for dots of different materials: perovskite, CdSe, InP and CdTe span visible colours; Si, InAs and PbS lie mostly in the infrared
options: Size tunes the colour only within one material: each material's band gap sets its range
PbS dots are always much larger than CdSe dots of the same quoted size
PbS absorbs all visible light, so it cannot give any out
Infrared light comes from heat, and PbS dots run hotter than CdSe dots
questions.explain: Small dots are bluer and large dots redder, but only within one material. Each material's band gap sets its range: CdSe covers the visible, PbS the infrared.
